atoms.text: Task 1  You will hear three people talking about educational justice. First, read the statements. Then listen to the audio file and match each speaker (1 to 3) with one of the statements.
atoms.sound: Task 1. You will hear three people talking about educational justice. First reed the statements. Then listen to the audio file and match each speaker with one of the statements.

instruction.sound: speaker 1 <voice voiceLang='en' voice='m2Us_chirp'>I believe education should be free at all levels, because financial barriers are the main reason why many talented students never reach university. If we want a fair society, we need to make sure that money doesn’t decide who gets an education.</voice> speaker 2 <voice voiceLang='en' voice='f3Us_chirp'>For me, the most important aspect of educational justice is equal access to high-quality schools. Right now, where you live often determines the quality of your education. That’s unfair, and it should not be allowed in a democratic society.</voice> speaker 3 <voice voiceLang='en' voice='f8Us_chirp'>I don’t think we should focus only on access. Support during the learning process is just as important. Many students from disadvantaged families need tutoring, mentoring, or simply encouragement. Without that, equal chances remain just a dream.</voice>

instruction.text: Task 2  You will hear a panel discussion between primary school teacher Bob Fisherman and education researcher Miranda Stuart on how to fight educational injustice. While listening, tick the correct answer. Only one answer is correct.
instruction.sound: Task 2. You will hear a panel discussion between primary school teacher Bob Fisherman and education researcher Miranda Stuart on how to fight educational injustice. While listening, tick the correct answer. Only one answer is correct.

atoms.sound: <voice voiceLang='en' voice='m9Us_chirp'>From my experience in the classroom, smaller class sizes would make the biggest difference. Teachers could give more individual attention and weaker students would benefit most.</voice> <voice voiceLang='en' voice='f10Us_chirp'>I agree individual support matters, but international studies show that reducing class size is extremely expensive and not always effective. We need to invest more in early childhood education — that’s where inequalities start, and that’s where interventions have the strongest long-term impact.</voice> <voice voiceLang='en' voice='m9Us_chirp'>But if we don’t improve the conditions in current classrooms, many students who are already disadvantaged will simply fall further behind.</voice> <voice voiceLang='en' voice='f10Us_chirp'>That’s why I think both early prevention and classroom improvements must go hand in hand, but the priority has to be breaking the cycle before it even begins.</voice>

atoms.a: What does the teacher see as the most effective way to improve educational justice?
b: More investment in early childhood education

atoms.a: According to the researcher, why should resources be spent on early childhood education?
b: Because it is cheaper than reducing class size.
Because children learn languages faster at that age.

atoms.a: Which difference between the two speakers is most obvious?
b: The teacher and the researcher disagree on whether education is important.
The teacher prefers more technology, the researcher prefers less.
++The teacher focuses on short-term classroom practice, while the researcher stresses long-term structural change.

instruction.text: Task 3  You are listening to an interview with the Minister of Education on the topic of educational equality. Listen to the audio file below and fill in the gaps, using the same exact wording used by the speakers.
instruction.sound: Task 3. You are listening to an interview with the Minister of Education on the topic of educational equality. Listen to the audio file below and fill in the gaps, using the same exact wording used by the speakers.

atoms.a: <voice voiceLang='en' voice='m3Us_chirp'>Minister, how do you evaluate the current situation of educational justice in our country?</voice> <voice voiceLang='en' voice='f1Us_chirp'>Well, we have made progress in recent years. More children from migrant backgrounds are finishing school successfully, and the number of students entering higher education has risen. However, we still see a strong link between social background and educational achievement. That means children from wealthier families still have a clear advantage. Our challenge is to close this gap through targeted support programs.</voice> <voice voiceLang='en' voice='m3Us_chirp'>So you’re saying poverty is still one of the strongest predictors of school failure?</voice> <voice voiceLang='en' voice='f1Us_chirp'>Exactly. If we don’t reduce the influence of family income on education, we will never reach true equality.</voice>

According to the minister, more children from ((migrant_backgrounds)) are now completing school successfully.
The minister admits that educational outcomes are still strongly influenced by ((social_background family_income poverty)) and ((social_background family_income poverty)).
In order to promote educational equality, the minister intends to set up targeted ((support_programs support_programmes)).
